The Lewinsky Scandal. The moment that exposed how one affair inside the White House could tear a nation apart along party lines.

Between 1995 and 1997, President Bill Clinton had a sexual relationship with Monica Lewinsky. She was an intern, only twenty-two or twenty-four years old, and the relationship happened inside and near the Oval Office itself. It remained secret for years.

Then came January 1998. Clinton was questioned under oath during a deposition for a sexual harassment lawsuit filed by Paula Jones. He was asked directly about the relationship, and he denied it. He claimed he had never had sexual relations with Lewinsky. It was a lie, told under oath in a legal proceeding.

But there was evidence. Linda Tripp had recorded conversations with Lewinsky. Those recordings ended up with Kenneth Starr, the independent counsel. When confronted with the recorded evidence, Clinton finally admitted to what he called "inappropriate relations."

Kenneth Starr released a detailed report. It was graphic. It detailed everything about the affair. On December 19, 1998, the House impeached Clinton on two charges: perjury and obstruction of justice. The nation watched as his presidency hung in the balance.

The Senate voted on the charges. On perjury, the vote was forty-five guilty to fifty-five not guilty. On obstruction, it was fifty to fifty. Neither came close to the sixty-seven votes needed for conviction. Clinton stayed in office.

But the damage was done. The scandal bitterly divided the country along partisan lines. It became a catalyst for intensifying the hostility between Congress members and deepened public distrust of institutions. Yet Clinton's approval rating remained high throughout the entire ordeal, which complicated the whole narrative. It showed the gap between what ordinary Americans thought and what political elites thought about the scandal. Bill Clinton was the president at the center. Monica Lewinsky was the intern whose affair precipitated the crisis. Kenneth Starr was the independent counsel who investigated and released the report. And the scandal became a major exercise of congressional power, a test of the impeachment process that ultimately changed how Americans viewed their government.
